# Craft laws

<!-- GENERATED from craft@0.1.0 (xag/craft-laws@26784a4). Do not edit this file.
     Edit the laws in craft/laws.py and re-render: `python -m craft.render > LAWS.md`.
     Editing the view is how a view becomes a second source of truth. -->

12 laws. **9 cite a source. 3 do not**, and are carried as hypotheses — visibly, and red in `craft.check`, until somebody sources them or deletes them.

Each law is stated as an observable, never as taste, so a verdict can be `fail` and not merely *I don't like it*. The **sightings** are the evidence: a law that has never caught anything is a law nobody should trust.

---

## NO-SYSTEM-VOCABULARY

The interface names things as the user names them, never as the system is built.

- **Violated by:** A word on screen that only the people who built it use.
- **Switched on by:** any interface at all; the app coins domain concepts of its own (a wall, a ledger, a charter)
- **Source:** [Nielsen Norman Group, 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design — #2 Match Between the System and the Real World](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ten-usability-heuristics/)
  > The design should speak the users' language. Use words, phrases, and concepts familiar to the user, rather than internal jargon.
- **Caught:** *chores 2026-07-13, the charter screen* — A section headed « Les murs » — a literal rendering of the codebase's own metaphor, 'hard walls'. A French parent does not set a wall; they forbid something. Now « Interdictions ».
- **Caught:** *chores 2026-07-13, the add-a-chore sheet* — « Tout l'équilibre se compte en minutes » — *l'équilibre* is the app's name for its own fairness ledger. A person counts minutes.

## SAYS-WHAT-HAPPENS

A control's label describes the action it performs.

- **Violated by:** A button labelled with a noun, a category, or the name of the section it sits in.
- **Switched on by:** any interface with a control that commits something
- **Source:** [GOV.UK Design System — Button](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/button/)
  > Write button text in sentence case, describing the action it performs… You may need to include more or different words to better describe the action.
- **Caught:** *chores 2026-07-13, the member sheet* — A section headed « Absence » whose submit button was also labelled « Absence ». In the English original: 'Away' over 'Away' — so the defect predated the translation by a year and nobody had ever read the screen.

## COMPOSED-PROSE

A sentence is one translatable unit; never assemble one from separately-translated fragments.

- **Violated by:** Any rendered line that is not a sentence a person would write. Judged AS RENDERED — never as an entry in a string catalogue, where each fragment is correct and the defect does not exist.
- **Switched on by:** the app is translated into any second language; any count, duration, date, currency or name is interpolated into a sentence
- **Source:** [Mozilla — Localization best practices for developers](https://mozilla-l10n.github.io/documentation/localization/dev_best_practices.html)
  > Splitting sentences into several keys often inadvertently presumes a grammar, a sentence structure, and such composite strings are unnecessarily difficult to translate… it is usually easier and quicker for translators to handle these as fixed strings rather than composed strings.
- **Caught:** *chores 2026-07-13, a proposal's countdown* — `proposal.closes` = « Encore {left} pour contester » composed with `left.min` = « encore {n} min », rendering « Encore encore 3 min pour contester. » Both strings correct in isolation. The defect existed only on the screen, and a catalogue of 304 strings cannot contain it.

## PLURALS-AND-AGREEMENT

Counts resolve through the target language's own plural rules, never through n == 1.

- **Violated by:** A hand-rolled `n === 1 ? singular : plural`; a form that is wrong at 0, 2, 11 or 21; a parenthesised gender ending shown to a reader (absent(e)).
- **Switched on by:** the app is translated into any second language; any count is shown to a person
- **Source:** [Unicode CLDR — Plural Rules](https://cldr.unicode.org/index/cldr-spec/plural-rules)
  > A common mistake is to think that 'one' is only for only the number 1. Instead, 'one' is a category for any number that behaves like 1. — six categories: zero, one, two, few, many, other.
- **Caught:** *chores 2026-07-13, the count on Today* — French treats 0 as singular (« 0 tâche »); English does not ('0 turns'). A binary check is wrong in the very first language you add. Routed through Intl.PluralRules.

In some languages the `one` category covers 1, 21 and 151 but not 11. The category is grammatical behaviour, not a number.

## GLOSSARY-FIRST

The domain nouns are settled BEFORE a word is translated, and settled by someone who speaks the target language — not by whoever commissioned the work, and not by the translator.

- **Violated by:** A glossary authored by the person requesting the translation. A domain noun that changes after translation has begun.
- **Switched on by:** the app is translated into any second language
- **Source:** [Lionbridge — How to create a translation style guide and terminology glossary](https://www.lionbridge.com/blog/translation-localization/how-to-create-a-translation-style-guide-and-terminology-glossary/)
  > Build a validated, client-approved glossary before a single word is translated.
- **Source:** [Creative Words — Terminology management in localization: why we never start with translation](https://www.creative-words.com/en/terminology-management-in-localization-why-we-never-start-with-translation/)
  > Terminology errors discovered late in the localization cycle require cascading fixes across all documents, all languages, and all versions.
- **Caught:** *chores 2026-07-13, every screen* — The commissioning agent invented « maisonnée » for *household* (literary; nobody says it) and counted chores in « tours » (« il reste 3 tours » — a board game), wrote both into the translator's brief as BINDING, and every tab, count and heading inherited them faithfully. The translation was executed perfectly. The words were wrong. A native speaker settled it in one question: équipe, and turns counted in tâches.

The failure mode is not a bad translator. It is a glossary nobody validated — and the person able to validate it is usually already in the room.

## TEXT-EXPANSION

Layout survives the target language's length — and SHORT strings are the dangerous ones.

- **Violated by:** Clipped or wrapped text in the target language at the narrowest real viewport.
- **Switched on by:** the app is translated into any second language; the app is used on a phone
- **Source:** [W3C — Text size in translation (citing IBM's globalisation guidelines)](https://www.w3.org/International/articles/article-text-size)
  > Up to 10 characters: 200–300% expansion. 11–20: 180–200%. Over 70: 130%. The smaller the source message, the higher the likely translation length.
- **Caught:** *chores 2026-07-13, the tab bar* — 'Today' (5) → « Aujourd'hui » (11). 'Household' → « Équipe ». The tab bar and the button row are the FIRST things to check, not the last — which is the opposite of the intuition that long paragraphs are the risk.

## NO-CALQUE  `UNCITED`

A metaphor is re-chosen in the target language, not carried across it.

- **Violated by:** A vivid source-language image that lands as jargon in the target language.
- **Switched on by:** the app is translated into any second language; the app coins domain concepts of its own
- **Source:** none found. This law is an assertion, not an authority — treat it as a hypothesis.
- **Caught:** *chores 2026-07-13, the households sheet* — « Ses propres habitants » — a *team* has no inhabitants. The word survived a glossary change from 'house' to 'team' because the sentences AROUND the changed word were never re-read.

Probably an instance of no-system-vocabulary rather than a law in its own right: a calqued metaphor is jargon in the target language. Kept separate because it is what actually goes wrong. Fold it in if it never earns a verdict of its own.

## UNTRANSLATABLE-TONE  `UNCITED`

A line whose only content is TONE may be dropped in a language with no equivalent register — not rendered.

- **Violated by:** A translated line that carries no information.
- **Switched on by:** the app is translated into any second language; the app's voice does work of its own (dry, warm, terse)
- **Source:** none found. This law is an assertion, not an authority — treat it as a hypothesis.
- **Caught:** *chores 2026-07-13, the empty board* — 'Nothing today. / That is the whole message.' — a dry joke about the app's own terseness. French has no such joke. Every attempt to carry it across produced a line that said nothing, and one of them — « Il n'y a rien à ajouter. » — sat forty pixels above a button marked AJOUTER. The fix was to let French decline the second line entirely.

This is the software-copy edge of transcreation, which is established practice in marketing localisation. I have not found it stated as a rule for UI copy. Source it or drop it.

## RARE-ACTION-FOLDS-AWAY

Frequency decides prominence; rare and advanced actions are deferred to a second layer.

- **Violated by:** The rarest action on a surface occupying the most space.
- **Switched on by:** a rare action shares a surface with frequent ones (create vs. switch; delete vs. edit)
- **Source:** [NN/g — Progressive Disclosure](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/progressive-disclosure/)
  > Initially, show users only a few of the most important options. Offer a larger set of specialized options upon request… the very fact that something appears on the initial display tells users that it's important.
- **Source:** [Nielsen Norman Group, 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design — #8 Aesthetic and Minimalist Design](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ten-usability-heuristics/)
  > Interfaces should not contain information that is irrelevant or rarely needed.
- **Caught:** *chores 2026-07-13, the households sheet* — Opened to SWITCH team; its largest element was a fully-expanded create-a-new-team form — an action performed about once a year. Folded behind a disclosure.

## ONE-SURFACE-ONE-JOB

A surface serves one intent; a second intent is a second surface, or a disclosure.

- **Violated by:** A person opening a surface for job A and being met by job B's form.
- **Switched on by:** a surface accumulates more than one intent (rename + configure + create)
- **Source:** [Nielsen Norman Group, 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design — #8 Aesthetic and Minimalist Design](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ten-usability-heuristics/)
  > Interfaces should not contain information that is irrelevant or rarely needed. Every extra unit of information in an interface competes with the relevant units of information.
- **Caught:** *chores 2026-07-13, the households sheet* — Three unrelated jobs stacked flat — rename this team, set its language, create another — plus a bare text box holding the team's name with nothing saying it was a name.

Weaker than the others as a standalone law: it derives from #8 and progressive disclosure, and so far it has never produced a verdict that rare-action-folds-away did not. Merge it if that holds.

## A-WAY-BACK

Every action a person can take by mistake has a marked exit.

- **Violated by:** A destructive or contested action with no undo, no cancel, and no way to object.
- **Switched on by:** an action is destructive, irreversible, or binding on somebody else
- **Source:** [Nielsen Norman Group, 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design — #3 User Control and Freedom](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ten-usability-heuristics/)
  > Users often perform actions by mistake. They need a clearly marked 'emergency exit' to leave the unwanted action without having to go through an extended process.

## EMPTY-STATE-NEVER-CONTRADICTS  `UNCITED`

No empty state asserts something the surrounding controls deny.

- **Violated by:** The zero state and a visible control disagreeing with each other.
- **Switched on by:** any surface has a zero state (a new user; a day with nothing due)
- **Source:** none found. This law is an assertion, not an authority — treat it as a hypothesis.
- **Caught:** *chores 2026-07-13, the empty board — the worst defect of the run* — « Il n'y a rien à ajouter. » rendered forty pixels above a button marked AJOUTER. As a sentence it is perfectly good French. It is absurd only in place, and no string table contains position.

A specific case of NN/g #4 (Consistency and Standards — 'users should not have to wonder whether different words, situations, or actions mean the same thing'), but I have not found it stated for empty states. It stays, uncited and red, because it caught the worst defect of the run — which is the only argument for a law that matters.

---

## The gate

Red, and correctly so: three of the twelve laws cite nobody. They are carried on purpose and they are visible — which is the whole difference between this and the markdown file it replaced, where the same three sat in a sentence that was true and could not fire. Discharge by finding the source, or by deleting the law. Never by editing this file.
